item.title: Electron spin relaxation and coherence times of silicon vacancies in 4H-SiC
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Low-concentration VSi centers in 4H-SiC reach maximum T1=42.8±1.3 ms and T2=0.708±0.004 ms on satellite transitions at T=80 K. Decoherence is governed by nuclear and spectral spin diffusion rather than electron spin-spin interactions.

Grade 0.428 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · Irene Donà, Michele Segantini, Gianluca Marcozzi, Nguyen Tien Son, Takeshi Ohshima, Ha Duong Ngo, Boris Naydenov

Figure

Electron spin coherence time T2 versus temperature T for central and satellite transitions. Experimental T2 rises linearly with decreasing temperature down to 80 K, with the satellite transition consistently yielding longer coherence times than the central transition.

Asks

What are the spin relaxation and decoherence mechanisms of silicon vacancy centers in 4H-SiC across T=80−300 K at low spin concentrations?

But

Spin concentrations cV1=1.47±0.3×1014 cm−3 and cV2=5.6±1.12×1013 cm−3; simplified theoretical diffusion model fails to reproduce the observed transition hierarchy and temperature dependence.

Tools

pulsed and continuous-wave X-band EPR · 808 nm optical hyperpolarization · electron irradiation (2 MeV) and annealing · EasySpin simulation

Abstract

Color defect centers carrying electron spins in solid crystals like diamond and silicon carbide (SiC) are promising candidates for qubits and quantum sensors, with SiC material being particularly interesting due to its compatibility with the existing semiconductor technology. Here we investigated the electron spin properties of silicon vacancy centers (V1 and V2) both electron spin S = 3/2 in 4H-SiC in the temperature range T=80-300~K using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). The EPR spectrum shows central and satellite lines, where the former ones originate from V1 and V2 centers, as well as from unknown defect center X. The analysis of continuous wave EPR measurements revealed a spin concentration of c_V1=1.47±0.3×10¹⁴, c_V2=5.6±1.12×10¹³ and c_X=1.03±0.21×10¹³ spins/cm³. Additionally, electron spin coherence T₂ and relaxation times T₁ have been measured on the central and on the satellite spectral lines, resulting in longer T₁ and T₂ for the satellite transition, compared to the central one, with maximum values of 42.8±1.3~ms and 0.708±0.004~ms respectively at T=80~K. We reveal, that decoherence is mainly caused by nuclear and electron spin diffusion.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Worth a look review — Lays out deployment targets for DOE fault-tolerant quantum computing: first-generation deployment in 2028 with ≥100 logical qubits executing 104 to 105 hard logical operations, scaling to 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits and 109 to 1010 operations in the 2030s.

Grade 0.416 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What roadmap, hardware targets, and software ecosystem does the US Department of Energy need to integrate fault-tolerant quantum computing into high-performance computing infrastructure by 2028 and beyond?

But

Strategic roadmap and policy planning document; targets contingent on experimental progress in physical qubit fidelity and logical error correction.

Tools

fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) roadmap · logical qubit architectures · DOE supercomputing infrastructure integration

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

item.title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
item.description:
Long shot new result — Trotterized Bosonic Qiskit simulation of a single polariton on an 8-site Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard chain tracks exact diagonalization with site occupation errors bounded between 10−4 and 10−2, peaking at 6.98×10−3.

Grade 0.403 · 1.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Nabaraj Khatri, Dilip Ojha, Rajib Tripathi, Kismat K. C, Ashish Khanal

Figure

Absolute occupation discrepancy |⟨ni⟩Trotter−⟨ni⟩Exact| versus time across 8 individual sites for a single initial polariton, showing saturation within 10−4 to 10−2.

Asks

Can Bosonic Qiskit with a Matrix Product State backend accurately capture many-body real-time dynamics in a Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard lattice when benchmarked against exact diagonalization?

But

One-dimensional open chains with Fock cutoff d=2 (hard-core photon limit), first-order Trotter decomposition with time step Δt=0.05, and restricted to low excitation numbers (1 or 2).

Tools

Bosonic Qiskit · Matrix Product State (MPS) backend · Trotterized circuit decomposition · Exact diagonalization benchmark

Abstract

The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.
